input:
## Scope

This review sets out to survey the rapidly growing literature on catalysts for the hydrogenation of carbon dioxide, a reaction that continues to attract enormous interest as a potential route for converting a waste gas into valuable products. The evidence base for the review consists of 82 papers published over the last 12 years. In broad terms, the reaction involves the conversion of carbon dioxide and hydrogen over a solid catalyst, and the products that are reported across the literature include methanol, methane, carbon monoxide, and higher hydrocarbons. The scope of the review is confined to thermal catalysis, and photochemical and electrochemical approaches, interesting though they are, fall outside it.

The catalyst families that are covered include copper-based catalysts, iron-based catalysts, and catalysts based on noble metals, along with the various supports and promoters that are reported in combination with them. Throughout the review, each paper's reported conversion and selectivity are treated as that author's own statement, made under the conditions that the author reports; where a paper happens not to state a particular condition, the review simply records the omission rather than attempting to supply the missing condition from elsewhere.

## Established results

There is a broad consensus in the literature regarding the general division of the field according to product. Copper-based catalysts are widely regarded as the established system for methanol formation, and their behaviour serves as the benchmark against which newer materials are typically reported. Iron-based catalysts, by contrast, tend to favour the hydrocarbon side of the product spectrum, ranging from methane through to longer-chain products. Noble-metal catalysts are generally reported as highly active systems, although the products they give are strongly dependent on both the metal and the support that is employed.

There is also widespread agreement that water is formed during the reaction and that this water has an effect on the catalyst. Although the direction of the effect varies from one system to another, its existence is not really in question: water is an inevitable product of the hydrogenation, it is present wherever conversion reaches appreciable levels, and a catalyst's ability to tolerate water forms part of its reported character. Another important point of consensus is the trade-off that exists between conversion and selectivity. Conditions that succeed in raising the conversion of carbon dioxide almost invariably shift the product distribution as well, and no report in the set manages to escape this trade-off entirely; the reports differ in where they judge the balance should be struck, rather than in whether such a balance exists at all.

It is further agreed that promoters and supports can change both the activity and the selectivity of a catalyst, in some cases by more than a change in the principal metal itself. The support must therefore be regarded as an integral part of the catalyst as reported, and any result that is stated for a metal in isolation should be treated as incomplete.

## Disagreements

One of the most notable areas of disagreement in the literature concerns the selectivity to methanol at a given conversion. When the comparison is made at matched conversion, some reports assign the higher selectivity to copper-based catalysts in their standard forms, whilst other reports assign it to modified or supported forms that their authors present as superior alternatives. Unfortunately, the set of papers does not resolve this conflict, largely because the conditions under which the various selectivities were measured differ from report to report in ways that are not always fully documented. The pressure, the feed composition, and the space velocity can each exert a significant influence on the selectivity, so a report that omits one of these variables cannot be compared exactly with a report that states it.

The disagreement also extends to the underlying source of the observed differences. One group of reports attributes the higher selectivity primarily to the state of the metal surface, whereas another group attributes it to the support and to the interface that exists between the metal and the support. These two attributions point towards quite different remedies, and the literature as it stands does not decide between them. The quantity that remains in conflict, therefore, is the selectivity itself, and until reports begin to state selectivity at matched conversion under fully documented conditions, the ranking of catalysts for methanol formation will remain an open question.

## Gaps

Perhaps the most striking gap in the literature is that the measurement nobody reports is the activity of the catalyst after extended time on stream. The papers in the set overwhelmingly report initial performance, that is, conversion and selectivity measured early on in a run using a fresh catalyst. By contrast, the behaviour of a catalyst following prolonged exposure to the reaction mixture, with water present and the feed flowing continuously, is recorded almost nowhere. Deactivation is a topic that is mentioned very frequently, yet it is measured only rarely, and no common, standardised way of reporting it has yet become established.

This gap has serious implications for every other part of the review, because the established results effectively rank catalysts according to their fresh performance, whereas a real plant does not operate with fresh catalyst indefinitely. A catalyst that leads the field in terms of initial selectivity but then loses its activity rapidly is a very different proposition from a catalyst with somewhat lower initial performance that nevertheless retains its activity over the long term, and the literature in its current state cannot reliably distinguish between these two cases. A standard long-run measurement, carried out and reported with the same degree of care as the initial measurements, would go a long way towards closing this gap, and its absence must be regarded as the single largest weakness of the present evidence base.

## Established results

Reports agree on the broad division of the field by product. Copper-based catalysts are the established system for methanol formation, and their behaviour is the reference against which newer materials are reported. Iron-based catalysts favour the hydrocarbon side of the product range, from methane towards longer chains. Noble-metal catalysts are reported mainly as highly active systems whose products depend strongly on the metal and on the support.

Reports also agree that water is formed in the reaction and that water acts on the catalyst. The direction of the action differs by system, but the presence of the action is not in dispute: water is a product of the hydrogenation, water is present wherever conversion is appreciable, and a catalyst's tolerance of water is part of its reported character. A further point of agreement is the trade-off between conversion and selectivity. Reports differ on where the balance should be struck, not on whether the balance exists.

The support is therefore part of the catalyst as reported, and a result stated for a metal alone is incomplete. Activity is reported on a variety of bases across the set, and the review has not forced the reports onto a single basis. Where the basis of a paper differs from the common practice of its family, the difference is recorded with the result. The agreement reported in this section survives those differences of basis: the agreement concerns the direction of effects and the division of the product range, and not the exact figures, on which the set varies widely.

## Disagreements

Reports conflict on the selectivity to methanol at a given conversion. At matched conversion, some reports assign the higher selectivity to copper-based catalysts in their standard forms, and other reports assign it to modified or supported forms that their authors present as superior. The set does not resolve the conflict, because the conditions under which the selectivities were measured differ between reports in ways the reports do not fully state. Another group attributes it to the support and to the interface between the metal and the support. The two attributions predict different remedies, and the set does not decide between them. The quantity in conflict remains the selectivity itself. Until reports state selectivity at matched conversion on fully stated conditions, the ranking of catalysts for methanol formation stays open. A smaller disagreement runs alongside the main one: whether selectivity should be compared at matched conversion at all, or whether each catalyst should be judged at its own best conditions. The review reports the conflict at matched conversion, because conversion itself moves selectivity, and a comparison that lets conversion float compares the conditions as much as the catalysts.

## Gaps

The measurement nobody reports is activity after extended time on stream. The papers in the set report initial performance: conversion and selectivity measured early in a run, on a fresh catalyst. The behaviour of a catalyst after long exposure to the reaction mixture, with water present and the feed running, is almost nowhere recorded. Deactivation is mentioned often and measured rarely, and no common form for reporting it has settled.

The gap limits every other part of the review. The established results rank catalysts on fresh performance; a plant does not run on fresh performance. A catalyst that leads on initial selectivity and loses activity quickly is a different proposition from a catalyst of lower initial performance that holds its activity, and the set cannot distinguish the two cases. A standard long-run measurement, reported with the same care as the initial measurements, would close the gap. Its absence is the largest single weakness of the evidence base.
